An agent of the local government has just gone to France from Montreal, at a cost of $5,000, to get servants of every description, and he has publicly advertised his mission. If there were a law in France against that kind of work, does my hon. friend think these operations would be possible ? I think not. How is it that the Minister of the Interior has never taken the trouble to ascertain definitely whether the laws of France allow that kind of work or not ? It is my belief that there is no law against it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Oh, yes, there is one, When I was in France I got a copy of the law, and I will send it to my hon. friend.
I would like to see it, because I do not think there is such a law that is put into operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Although the test of the law has not been sent by Mr. Wiallard, he refers to it in his last report, where he says :
In regard to the question of publicity, as we have already said elsewhere, we cannot make a very active propaganda by means of the press, as is done in England and in the countries where no prohibitive law exists; we enjoy, however, a certain liberty in this respect, of which we shall know how to take advantage, as we have done before. Newspaper articles, distribution of pamphlets having only an historic, geographic, or economic character, and consequently not giving rise to any objection on the part of the authorities, notices drawing the attention of the public to the existence of the office of the Commissioner General for Canada, always ready to give official information as to the advantages ofiered to certain classes of emigrants; such are the means we have employed up to now and which we count on using further and on a larger scale, to accentuate still further and to increase the favour which our country enjoys in France.

This of course does not give us any information as to the real state of the law. It is quite possible that there exists in France some prohibition against actually seducing a man out of his own country and taking him abroad. There are several countries in Europe where it is not allowed to induce a man by false representations to leave the country and go to another country. Rut this is a different matter, and Mr. Wiallard's opinion as to the extent to which the law goes in France is worth nothing. It is surprising that none of these agents that we have in France should have sent a report, giving us the exact state of the French law on this subject. If it is forbidden to carry on any propaganda in France, why are we spending thousands of dollars every year to maintain agents for the purpose of carrying on that propaganda? My hon. friend says we are doing it cautiously. Well, I must say that I do not like that way of doing things. It reminds me of the mysterious contract
with the North Atlantic Trading Company, under which we paid thousands of dollars to agents for the purpose of carrying on a propaganda, and when we wanted to have the names of those agents, my hon. friend, the incarnation of Liberalism in the province of Quebec, voted that we should not have their names and applauded when his leader, the Prime Minister, expressed a fear that they might commit suicide if they were discovered. Does my hon. friend think there is any danger of our young and jovial friend Mr. Geoffrion committing suicide? Oh. no. I entirely approve of the system they have in the United States, and I venture to think, without being a prophet, that we shall have the same system here before long. They forbid all immigration propaganda. They do not spend a single cent to employ people in foreign countries to induce other people to come to the United States. They have never for a single moment entertained such a policy. They consider it undignified. They make their country and its progress known by judicious advertising at world exhibitions, and I venture to say that the United States as a country of settlement is much better known in France than Canada is. So that for my own part I do not at all approve of the system of having immigration agents anywhere. But if we have them in France, we ought to act openly with them. If there is a law there forbidding them, we ought to withdraw them. We pay a considerable sum for these agents, and we ought to know the work they are doing. The fact that they are residing in Paris does not satisfy me that they are employing their time continuously for the purpose of advancing the cause of immigration.

My hon. friend knows that their work is not confined to Paris. The office of Mr. Fabre is in France, but these agents go into different provinces to do their work, returning on Saturday1 night to Paris.

My hon. friend knows that Mr. Wiallard has his residence and his office in Paris. I do not know whether Mr. Geoffrion resides in Paris or not. I assume that he does, from those very interesting letters w7hich he has been sending to the French papers in Montreal, which are dated from Paris, and from which it abundantly appears that his excursions into the provinces do not necessitate his being absent from Paris very long; and in Paris there is not very much immigration work to be done. What alarmed me most in my hon. friend's statement was the announcement that we were going to have immigration agents in each county in the province of Quebec. Is the system which has existed in the province of Ontario of having agents in each county going to be duplicated in the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: Certainly. -
I am not aware that those agents have been a success in Ontario, and I am afraid that the system will not work much better In Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: The farmers of Ontario are very much pleased with It.

I do not think it has served the purpose for which it was established. It was established for the purpose of enabling certain political friends of the government in Ontario the opportunity of making a little money.
. Mr. OLIVER. Will my hon. friend tell me the source of his information that the system of distribution agents in Ontario has been a failure?

I have seen in the papers a very severe criticism of the system, and one of those agents, I think, was arrested and is being prosecuted in Ontario. I am against all this kind of immigration expenditure. In- Ontario it has been resorted to for the purpose of giving encouragement to political friends, and I have no doubt whatever that if the system is now introduced in Quebec, it is for the same object.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does it encourage my hon. friend's political supporters to prosecute them?

When they are caught with their hands in the cash box, they have to be brought to justice. I think if we were to prosecute all those who waste part of that million and odd dollars spent on immigration, the minister would be kept very busy indeed. We have agents in the eastern townships, and my hon. friend has consented to add to the number by appointing agents in other parts in the province of Quebec, and he consented to do all this because of representations made to him by gentlemen on his side that he must do to the rest of the province of Quebec what he has been doing so abundantly for Ontario the past year or turn. I do not think he will deny that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What evidence has my hon. friend of this aggressive attitude on the part of the province of Quebec ?

It is very difficult to give evidence on that point. It is, in that respect, like many other things everybody speaks of, which we hear about in the corridors of this House, which we see hinted at in the organs of hon. gentlemen opposite in the province of Quebec, but if we arVasked to do, as we are asked every day in the Public Accounts Committee-if we are asked to produce the best written and absolute proof, such as is required in a court of justice, of course we cannot do it. But there is no one in the province of Que-Mr. MONK.
bee who has any doubt about what I have asserted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My objection was to the assertion of my hon. friend that it required an aggressive attitude in order to bring to my mind a case of injustice, if one should exist.

My hon. friend the Postmaster General said last year that there was no immigration from France. I am glad to see him back here so that I may remind him. He said last year that it was useless to seek immigration from France because Frenchmen do not emigrate.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: My hon. friend must not put words in my mouth which I did not utter. I have no hesitation in saying that of all the countries of Europe, France is probably the one which sends the fewest emigrants to foreign countries. I base my opinion on all authorities who have written of late on the subject, and my hon. friend knows perfectly well that such is the case. But I am in favour of desirable French immigration. It will come in a limited number, but if we can capture that limited number, so much the better. We are doing our best in that respect, and we have met on this side of the House from the hon. gentleman who is at the head of the Department of the Interior, and we also did from his predecessor, much sympathy and the best encouragement possible.
I notice that my (hon. friend is very generous in the praise he bestows on the Minister of the Interior. He even went so far as to praise the previous encumbent of the office.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: I am only stating the truth. And I am saying this because my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) and his immediate predecessor have been greatly misrepresented in the province of Quebec as being deadly opposed to all French immigration. Why should they be ? As a matter of .fact they have not. We have received from both the best possible encouragement ; but even with the best possible encouragement, as I said last year, we cannot expect a very large flow of immigrants from the country of our ancestors.

That eulogium of the previous minister is very significant ?' A|re we to infer that he is coming back ? My hon. friend will remember that when the previous minister (Mr. Sifton), towards whom he is so generous to-night, resigned, my hon. friend's organ in Montreal made a terrible attack on him ; and among other accusations was this very one, which no doubt emanated from my hon. friend or his neighbour the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), and which went to say

that he had been bitterly opposed to all French immigration ever since he was made head of the Department of the Interior.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: I never realized how apt is the good English expression ' a fig-menlt of the imagination.' This is indeed a figment of my hon. friend's imagination.
My hon. friend knows very well what appeared in his organ in Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: I have no organ there unfortunately.

He has a very noisy and turbulent organ in Montreal, and at the time attacks appeared in it, emanating either from my hon. friend or his neighbour the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who both inspire that organ, and the gravamen of these accusations, which appeared every morning against the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) at that time, was that the government were obliged to get rid of him because he was so much opposed to French immigration. Now my hon. friend tells us that he noticed at all times how friendly that hon. gentleman was to that particular branch of the service. My hon. friend says that there are not many emigrants who leave France. That is not what Le Yicomte d'Avanel says. My hon. friend has just referred to that eminent writer.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: He deplores the fact that so few Frenchmen avail themselves of the immense opportunities which are to be found in the western states.
What he deplores is that they have not taken their share in the immense prosperity of the west.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: Hear, hear.

And I would infer from his remarks that Frenchmen have not been conspicuous in the development of the west, but I would not infer that they had not emigrated in fair quantities. Another thing remarkable is that he does not point out that there is any law against French emigration. My hon. friend will remember that quite lately in an article in ' La Revue des deux Mondes,' one of the leading French periodicals, written by one of our French lecturers in Montreal, on French emigration-although there are many inaccuracies in his article-he does not refer in any way to the laws of Franee as being opposed to emigration from that country. My hon. friend was mistaken in saying that there were more immigrants came from France to Canada than came from France to the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: In proportion.

The proportion of immigration is much larger from Italy, Russia and 313
Germany. But my hon. friend would be astonished, if he took up the four last reports of the immigration commissioner of United States, to see by the valuable compilations of statistics there, how many Frenchmen have migrated to the United States. As a practical conclusion, I would like a statement from the Minister of the Interior that we are to have more extended reports from Mr. Wiallard and his associates in the future. The report given in my hon. friend's return covers scarcely two pages and is in such general terms that it merely conveys no information whatever of a valuable kind.

I see that this same amount of $200,000 was appropriated for this service in 1907-8. But in the Auditor Generals' Report, I cannot find any distinction between the salaries under this head and other expenses. How much was actually spent in salaries last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The whole vote was expended, $200,000.	.
But did $200,000 cover all the salaries of the agents and employees in Canada, Great Britain and foreign countries ? Or was it necessary to get a further sum from some other source ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are some other things besides that are paid out of contingencies.

Under what authority is the minister able to pay salaries out of contingencies ? I want to know exactly what was spent last year under this item of the estimates, and from what sources the money came and by what authority ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I say that the sum spent under this item is $200,000.
But I want to know the sum spent on this service : 1 Salaries of agents and employees in Canada, Great Britain and foreign countries.'

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The information is not arranged just in that way, but I may be able to give the answer in a few miuutes.
Has the minister with him the list of booking agents in France to whom we have given the privilege of earning this bonus 1

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: Currie & Son, Hernu & Perron and Pitt & Scott. Each agency has ten subagencies in France, making thirty subagents who are working in our interest.
I can scarcely understand that. For, the evidence we had before the committee on immigration led me to believe that we had only three certified or authorized booking agents in France.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: Bnt they have subagents.
Carried.

But we find that in the British isles, every hooking agent must take out a license, and every licensed booking agent in the British Isles has the authority of this government to earn the bonus. And there are hundreds of them.
I hear some hon. gentlemen crying * carried.' Perhaps the subject of immigration does not interest them. But it interests us, and the subject ought to be examined somewhat carefully before we vote a million dollars for the service. We are entitled to get information, even if somebody is driven to commit suicide.
I say that, in England, every licensed booking agent is the authorized agent of this government. He receives circulars showing the advantages he may reap by selling tickets to Canada to get the bonus. In France, there are only three agents. If it is a country where it is worth our while to recruit, why do not we have a sufficient propaganda ? What is the use of having three booking agents in Paris, if, as the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) says, the really good immigration is to be found in the Basque provinces or in the Norman country ? Why not have your booking agents in Rouen, in the centre of Normandy ? And if the Basques are good immigrants, why have not you booking agents in the cities of that region ? Why have not Mr. Wiallard and these other gentlemen whose salaries we are paying, taken an interest in this matter ? If this system of $5 a head and $2 for babies is a good system, why not carry it out in a proper way, in every country in which we think it worth while to carry it on at all ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The booking ageut, both in England and in France, is licensed as my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) has said : The booking agent may have a number of subagencies. For instance, my hon. friend has heard of the booking agency firm of Cook & Son, in England, Scotland, France, Belgium, Holland, and, I suppose, every other European country. These people have numerous agencies throughout the British islands, to say nothing of the continent, but it is the firm of Cook & Son that is responsible to the British government for all these agencies. In France, there is the firm of Pitt & Scott, which has subagencies in all parts of the country. But it is the firm itself which puts up the security witli the French government and is responsible to the government for the conduct of those agencies. Because there is only one firm of Pitt & Scott, it does not follow that there is only one point at which that firm sells tickets to Canada. There are three firms in all with which we Mr. MONK.
are doing business in France, and each of these has subagents. We do not deal with the subagencies, but with these firms, because we believe them to be reliable firms, firms who will not get us into trouble with the French government or deal improperly with the immigrants. They are responsible people, as we understand it. Whatever is being done is done in the open light of day, and will be. We believe that by dealing with responsible firms we are achieving a measure of publicity which we could not achieve in any other way at the same price. With regard to the inquiry by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake), there is a contingency vote out of which we paid last year about $7,000 in salaries. I cannot give a detailed statement of the balance of the contingency vote, because it was out of this vote that we pay the detention hospital charges, which charges are recouped to us, in many cases, by the steamship companies.
Am I correct in assuming that the $207,000 will cover all the salaries of last year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Is a bonus still being paid on Galicians coming to this country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. we have no booking agencies operating in Austria-Hungary.

At one time the government gives one explanation and at another time a totally different one. When this question of paying bonuses was discussed, my hon. friend stated, and the superintendent General of Immigration stated at that time in an interview he gave to the ' Globe ' newspaper, and we by no means paid this bonus to anybody who sold a ticket to an immigrant for Canada. There had to be a selection, and if a man was found qualified he got an authorization from this government, and that man alone could receive the bonus. Now what are the facts as revealed to us this evening? They are quite different. Every booking agent in the British Isles can earn a bonus, there is no special authorization of any kind given. The mere fact of the booking agent receiving the little package of circulars in which this bonus system is made known to him, constitutes his authorization. Therefore every booking agent in the British Isles who has a license to sell tickets is ipso facto authorized by this government. That admission was made by the Superintendent General of Immigration before our Committee on Agriculture. Now on the continent it is different. I saw by the evidence given before the Agricultural Committee, and by the documents of the committee, that we had three booking agents in Paris. It now turns out by a statement which seems to

have no foundation-1 mean to say that it does not seem to result from anything that has been put before this House-that through these three agencies in Paris we extend our ramifications for bonus all over France. Is that the case? Are these men at the sub-agencies, whose names are not known to us, authorized to collect a bonus? We had a statement previously that only the man who is examined, found qualified and specially authorized by this government, would get the bonus. Now to-night we are told that there are over forty agencies throughout France.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think that any number of sub-agencies in France was mentioned.

The Postmaster General said that each of these three agencies had ten sub-agencies. Where did the hon. gentleman find that out?-because we had the testimony under oath of the head officer of the department in the Committee of Immigration that we had three agents, and their names were given.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: When was that evidence taken before the committee?
A few days ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: There is no discrepancy between the statements. There are three large firms in Paris, Pitt & Scott, Currie & Son, and Hernu & Perron. Hernu & Perron have their central office in Paris, just in front of the Canadian office, Rue de Rome. It is well known that they have sub-agents in every large city of France. I saw the names published this summer. Take the Cooks, for example. A firm like the Cooks has an agency in every city and every town of France.
Does the hon. gentleman pretend that if Cooks in London are our authorized agents, all Cooks' sub-agents can earn the bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: I say that those three agents get the premium, and they are interested in getting as many as possible from the different suboffices all the same. They will get the premium on every immigrant they bring from any portion of France, not only from the place where they have their central office. They have agencies all over France. A firm like Hernu & Perron has agencies at Bordeaux, at Marseille, at Dunkerque and at Havre, in fact in every large port of France, and the whole staff of every sub-agency is working for the central agency in Paris.

I pretended that was the case when I discussed the motion for the abolition of the bonus, and my hon. friend the minister sternly denied it. He said that we only had agents specially authorized. The Postmaster General says that 3131
Cook & Company are the greatest booking agents in Europe; and he says that Hernu & Perron in Paris have sub-agents everywhere. Therefore the sub-agents are entitled to earn the bonus.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: No, I hope the hon. gentleman is not playing upon words. I say that these immigrants which are being gathered by the sub-agencies of Hernu & Perron, entitle Hernu & Perron to the premium on those immigrants. Whether they are gathered by Hernu & Perron in Paris, or whether they are gathered beyond Paris by the sub-agents, it is the firm of Hernu & Perron which gets the premium.

That is what I argued at the time. Now what is the consequence of the minister's statements? Cook & Sons in London, Cook & Sons in Glasgow, and Cook & Sons in Aberdeen are authorized agents entitled to collect the bonus. Now surely their sub-agents are in the same position, and they earn the bonus also.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: Hernu & Perron's agents are paid by them, not by the government.

Therefore it follows that Cook & Sons agencies all over the continent of Europe, wherever the bonus is authorized to be paid, earn the bonus. Does the Minister of the Interior admit that the proposition of the Postmaster General is well founded?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will try again to explain the situation. My hon. friend has said that Cook & Sons in the British islands are entitled to the bonus under certain conditions as other booking agents in the British islands are.
They are authorized to collect the bonus.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend says that they are allowed to collect the bonus.
Because ail licensed agents are.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As a matter of fact all licensed agents are not because for cause we refuse to deal with certain booking agents.
If they rob you, of course, you do not deal with them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not only if they rob us but if they do not act properly we refuse to do business with them. But as a rule what my hon. friend says is correct, that licensed booking agents in Great Britain and Ireland are entitled to secure the bonus under certain conditions. That condition prevails in the British Isles because there is no restrictive law agaiDSt immigration, but, on the continent of Europe, because of the restrictive laws, we do not make a general.

automatic arrangement with all booking agents. We only deal with those whom we consider reliable and satisfactory. We select in those countries the agents whom we will do 'business with. In the British Islands we select those whom we will not do business with. Cook & Sons are not those whom we have selected to do business with in France or on the continent.
It seems that it is very difficult for me to make my reasoning clear to the hon. gentleman. We have agents in Faris to the number of three ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
They have sub-agents all over France and when these sub-agents book emigrants to Canada the head office collects the bonus ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
We have Cook & Sons in London and when Cook & Sons book an immigrant to Caanda they collect the bonus ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Cook & Sons in the British Islands but not Cook & Sons in France, Belgium, Holland or anywhere else on the . continent.
Why not ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Because we have no agreement with Cook & Sons.

You have no agreement
with Hernu & Perron. Your arrangements are the same as you have with your English agents. You have no special arrangement differing from that which you have with your English agents.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are appointed by us as our agents. They are selected by us to act as our agents just the same as we select certain agents in Great Britain to act in Great Britain for us.
The hon. gentleman is simply playing on words. There Is no appointment and my hon. friend knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will not continue the discussion with the hon. gentleman as a matter of argument but I want to state to him as a matter of fact that we do not pay Cook & Sons a bonus on each immigrant booked by them from France.

Well, there is no appointment of agents. When we were put under that impression some weeks ago it was entirely erroneous unless you call an appointment the fact of giving a booking agent three or four circulars in which it Is shown that he can obtain the bonuses by booking to Canada railway navvies, farm labourers, farmers, and domestic servants. Does the Mr. OLIVER.
mere fact of our immigration agent giving the booking agent these circulars constitute his appointment? Hernu & Perron and Currie & Sous in Paris have the same appointment as the booking agents in the British Islands in that they get these circulars in which it is shown that they can get $5 or $2 a head for immigrants of a certain class. We' pay a bonus, under the terms of out-order in council to immigrants from Galicia. The order in council covers German Galicia ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
And Russian Galicia ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Sure.
Mi*. MONK. But my hon. friend says that wb do not pay any bonus because we have no booking agents there. What I want to know is this : Cook & Sons have agents all over Galicia and in all those countries ; supposing they get their immigrants booked through Cook & Sons in London what is to prevent Cook & Sons of Paris from claiming the bonus through Cook & Sons in London ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Our arrangement is that the booking agent can only claim bonus on a citizen of the country in which he is a booking agent.
I say that there is no such indication in their appointment whatever. If I can be shown that there is I will retract that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Our circular to booking agents makes that distinct statement for the very reason that my hon. friend has suggested to the House.

There is a suggestion in the circular that the bonus is paid to the booking agent himself and not to any subagent. I remember that suggestion but that is not what the Postmaster General has told us this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The circular most distinctly points that out and it is in the circular for the definite purpose of preventing what my hon. friend suggested a little while ago-a booking agent say, in Antwerp, collecting commission on an immigrant from some other country than Belgium. A booking agent in Antwerp can only collect commission upon people of Belgian citizenship.
Has my hon. friend a circular with him ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, I am not able to give the hon. gentleman evidence of that fact but that is the statement as I remember it iu the circular. However, that is the administration for the very obvious reasons

that he has already placed before the committee.
Of course, if it is in the circular we can find it, but my recollection of the circular is that it forbade the right of a booking agent to get the bonus through any other person whatever.

The hon. Minister of the Interior said a while ago, in answer to my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), that he was of the same opinion regarding paying bonuses that he held a few years ago. Well, that may be so, but if so the minister has changed his method of expressing his ideas because, as far as my recollection goes, and I think I have refreshed my memory by reading the hon. gentleman's speech, he denounced in toto the bonus system in the old country. He declared distinctly that the payment of bonuses to the steamship companies and the payment of bonuses to permanent agents in the old country was money worse than wasted, and the only feature of the immigration policy he did not condemn was the sending of farm delegates from Canada to the mother country. I understand the Minister of the Interior has continued sending delegates to the old country to whom he pays $100 per month and expenses. Probably some of these farm delegates have induced immigrants to come to Canada, but some of them not being practical farmers themselves proved of doubtful benefit to the country. Some were clergymen, some residents of towns who knew nothing about farming, but they had a nice jaunt at the expense of the government and a salary of $100 per month besides. Can the minister give me the names of the farm delegates who were sent to the old country in 1907 ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
About 20 were sent but I am sorry I have not the names at hand.
I will give them later.
Were they selected from each province in the Dominion ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, except from the maritime provinces.
. Mr. W. J. ROCHE. Has the minister any figures to show the number of immigrants which each delegate has induced to come out ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be impossible to give the result of their work in the actual number of immigrants who came here. We get a report from the delegate showing in such detail as may be where he has been and the means taken by him to present the advantages of Canada to the British public. We expect that the presentation of the ad-1 vantages of Canada by a credible representative will have an effect beyond the mere1 fact of his presence, and that at a later date people will come to Canada who have been influenced by him. My hon. friend will agree that it is not the man who is most easily moved to emigrate who makes-the best settler ; possibly the man who is slowest to move is the better man after we secure him. True we may have made' mistakes. We desire to give a reasonably fair and equal representation to the various provinces with a special preponderance to the prairie provinces. We have to get men as we can, and I am sorry to say the selections have not always been entirely the best. But taking it year by year and considering all the circumstances the system is thoroughly justified by its results. We have been able by this means to bring the agricultural advantages of Canada directly before the population of the British Isles in a way that we could not otherwise do. Our eiforts are particularly directed to get people who will settle on the land and the difficulty in former years was that the advantages of Canada had been brought prominently before those who were not fitted to take advantage of our conditions. So far as we have been able to follow, the work of the agricultural delegates it has been eminently satisfactory, and those who have come as a result of their mission have been in the majority of oases the very people Canada wants and is quite willing to spend money to get.
Have the labours of the delegates been confined to the British Isles ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One has gone to France, one to Belgium, and one or two more will go.
Who went to Belgium ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Morel.
What time of the year was he sent ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: November or early in December.
Was he a native of Belgium ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
What qualifications must these men possess ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have to do the best we can, but the qualifications we ask are that the man shall be an actual farmer, that he shall be a successful farmer, and if possible a native of the country to which he goes.
I suppose he must have farmed on the prairie for a time ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, he must be a man who has made a success of practical farming in this country.
What is the policy of paying the farmers ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Last year we sent them immediately after the new year, to remain three mouths, and we paid them $100 a month and their expenses during their absence from home. We found, however, that the season was rather short, because these men, being engaged in practical farming, had to be at home on their places early in the spring. So that this year we tried to get them away in December. The period is three or possibly four months.

I feel a little sensitive on this point of immigration from Belgium, because I made efforts last fail to get a very successful farmer in my constituency, Mr. Hardy, of Hartney, sent there, and after trying for two months, I found that he could not be sent. I think that one of the important qualifications of these men is that they must be Grits.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: They are the people who talk well of the country.
They have always a pleasant smile. Who went to France ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry that I am unable to give the name of the man who went this year. The delegate who went last year was Mr. Vauriot. Both of them wTere from Manitoba.
'ROCHE (Marquette). How long has the system of paying $100 a month been in vogue ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say at the moment when it was made a system. It has been the practice ever since I have been in the department, and I think some time before. At first I think there was a system of sending what were called returned men, that is to say, men who had come from the old country a few years before and who wished to make a visit home. They were given a free passage back or some slight assistance in that way. But it was found that that was not satisfactory, and it was decided that if we were to get good service we would have to send men whose time was worth something to them, that is, men in actual business, who could not afford to go simply for fun, and we had to pay them something as a salary, so that they could provide for filling their places at home while they were absent. They were placed at the disposal of our regular agents, to go and come and give their services as they were required. Although that appears to be more costly than the other way, we believe that we get more value for our money.

The reason I ask that question is that about a year ago I met one of these returned farm delegates on a political platform. The preced-Mr. OLIVER.
ing speaker had twitted him with having received a considerable amount from the government as a delegate, but he rather repudiated the idea and posed as a philanthropist, saying that he had only got his expenses. However, I find in the Auditor General's Report that even this gentleman is down for $100 a month ; so that he must have had a slip of the memory. I wish to ask the minister if the government has been assisting any needy settlers in the province of Manitoba within the last year by buying provisions for them ? If so. in what portion of the province do they reside, who made the request, and what quantities of provisions were dispensed ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it has been unfortunately necessary this year to provide some assistance in what are called the Toulon and Gimli districts in the eastern part of the province. That is the only part of the province where it has been necessary to give assistance.
What did the provisions consist of ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could give the hon. gentleman a complete return. The principal supply was flour, in addition to which there were some small articles which were absolute necessities.
What security has the government ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have taken a lien on the homestead as security for the advance.
Who was it made the request for assistance ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A petition was received from the locality, and the case was investigated by our officers, and it was decided that it was a proper action to take.
The minister would not object to bring dowu that petition ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no.

The reason I ask about this is that I saw an article in a newspaper of the district in which these provisions were distributed, stating that it was felt by many that while there may have been a few deserving families requiring assistance, advantage had been taken of the distribution by some of the government agents there to get a hold on these people, and to use this distribution, like the distribution of seed grain, as a political lever. It was" reported that the advances were held back until an election was on, and that they were then used for the purpose of influencing votes. In the method of distribution of this flour among the Galicians and other foreigners the object seems to purchase their votes in that

way. Let me read an article which appeared in a Selkirk paper :
Surely the elections are not very far distant. They are casting their shadows before them in the shape of three or five carloads of flour sent by the government for the foreigners at Gimli and Winnipeg beach. These people are getting too wise to be inveigled in this way, as they find out it is to be charged up against them when they receive the patents for their lands, or in other words they are expected to pay for their own election bribes, and many of them are refusing to take any of it. It looks like another election dodge such as was acted upon at the last provincial election when innumerable patents were granted to those who had complied with the requirements and the duties of a homesteader on condition that they cast their votes for the Liberal candidate. The game was to hold off granting these patents until election times and then to convince the foreigners that it was a gift if they put up the goods on election day, although they were entitled to these patents some time before.
According to that article inducements in the shape of distributions of flour were held out to those who were really not in need of it in order to get their votes. I am aware that there has been purchased from the Lake of the Woods Milling Company some $870 worth of flour, distributed amongst those foreigners, to say nothing of over $400 worth got for the same purpose from the Ogilvie Milling Company, and a good many of these foreigners repudiated the idea that they were in need at all. No one is going to condemn the distribution among needy settlers, but there were comparatively few that required this distribution. Whatever truth there may be in this article, those in charge of the distribution will be better able to tell. Who did distribute this flour?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Having seen probably the same article my hon. friend has read, we had a further report made, and will be able to present the whole of the facts to the House to-morrow, as well as the names of the officials who made the distribution.
When was it made?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In January and February of this year.

Among the Canadian immigration agents appear the names of a large number of officials at Ottawa, such as Mr. Bryce, Mr. C. H. Beddoe, Mr. Dan McGillicuddy, and others. Are they paid as agents $100 per month and expenses besides their usual salary, and how long are they kept on the other side?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Dr. Bryce is the chief medical officer of the department. He has charge of the hospitals and of the examinations for medical fitness at the ocean ports. He is also medical officer for the Indian Department. Mr. Beddoe is chief accountant for the Interior Department. As such he went to Europe to investigate the accounts of the North Atlantic Trading Company and was paid his travelling expenses in that connection.

Two hundred and ten dollars are charged for his expenses in that connection. One would judge from the Auditor General's Report that all those mentioned went to Europe. Mr. W. W. Cory obtained an advance for travelling expenses. Dr. Bryce also appears in the list of Canadian agents of immigration and was paid $450 expenses. Then I think my hon. friend to the left must have been mistaken when he said they must all be Reformers, because I find in the list the Hon. Frank Oliver $2,900 for travelling expenses. We always looked upon him as an Independent.
I suppose he went to the old country also.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The gentlemen whose names have been mentioned receive a good deal more than $100 a month, and these expenses are in addition to their salaries.
How long would they remain in the old country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The farm delegates remain generally about three months. Dr. Bryce did not go to the old country. Mr. Beddoe went to Amsterdam in connection with the North Atlantic Trading Company's contract, and I think he remained there three or four days. I was absent some seven months from Canada.

Mr. Smith, formerly of Winnipeg, head of the immigration branch there, was transferred to the old country and Mr. Bruce Walker brought over in his place, but why was the transfer made, and what are their respective salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The salaries are the same in both cases, $3,000. Mr. Smith was getting $3,000 in Winnipeg and Mr. Walker $3,000 in London, with $600 living allowance in addition. Mr. Walker desired to change his location on account of the health of his wife with whom the English climate did not agree, and Mr. Smith desired to change his on account of the health of a member of his family with whom the climate of Manitoba did not agree.

I desire to bring to the attention of the minister a matter which is mentioned almost every session, but which will stand repetition particularly upon the eve of an expected election. I refer to the part that immigration and other officials of the department are taking in politics. Notwithstanding that this parliament unanimously passed a resolution a few years ago-acquiesced in by the minister-declaring that no civil servant shall take part in elections, I received 1 information from numerous sources that the

98.71
hon. minister's officials are taking an active part in elections at this moment. During the past few weeks, a Galician interpreter connected with the Interior Department, is making a house to house canvass in the Galician colony in my constituency. This took place last election and has taken place at intervals since, and the same is now going on. The expectation is that he would get a number of these people naturalized- and that is another thing, commissioners appointed under the Naturalization Act passed by this parliament, have been going there taking their naturalization papers and rounding the people up together to get them registered, and taking a very active partisan part in politics. When I was coming through Winnipeg, a month or so ago, I heard that two or three officials had been amongst the foreign population in the northern part of Alberta and iSaskatchewan. I am sure that the minister, personally, would like to see the mandate of this parliament obeyed, therefore, I call this matter to his attention. But immigration agents and others do not of their own volition and without some instruction from their superior officers, carry on such work as this. The minister may not be cognizant of it, but some of his officers must be, and they must have taken it upon themselves to direct these immigration agents to take this active part in politics.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman give me the name of the interpreter of whom he speaks ?

Of course, the old stand-by is always there, Philip Harvey. But he is not the one I speak of as being in my own constituency at the present time. I have not under my hand the letter telling about this man, but my recollection is that his name is Genik or something like that. I can let the hon. minister know.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would like to have the name. I have already said in this House, and I say again, that I do not think the government stands to profit by political activity on the part of its employees; and, so far as I am concerned, I object entirely to that activity. I have addressed a letter to the employees of the department warning them against taking an active part in politics. I should be very glad to have information from any of our friends on the other side in regard to improper activity on the part of our officials, and I will find out whether my instructions can be carried put or not.

What is the penalty ? No doubt, the minister is sincere in this, and yet, though we bring the matter to the attention of the minister, these officials still go on as before. What does the minister do when he finds that his instructions have been disregarded ? I have already referred Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
in this House to cases of which I know. I can give names to-night if necessary of public officials whose principal occupation is canvassing for elections. The minister says he would like information, but, if he is given the information, what penalty will he inflict? Will he dismiss the official ? There is no doubt of the facts-these men in Manitoba, in the Northwest and in British Columbia are continually canvassing for election.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The only penalty we can enforce is dismissal from the service. Of course, that would not be done without careful inquiry, and our friends opposite would not expect us to dismiss a man unless the eivdence is clear. Certainly they wpuld not expect us to dismiss him on mere report. That is why I said I would like the name and occasion, so that I could bring the matter fco an issue. And, of course, lion, gentlemen opposite may be to some extent mistaken and may believe that certain action is taken when it is not taken. I suppose they will admit that there is a possibility of even themselves being somewhat biased in their view as to the action of officials. It has been absolutely necessary that our officials in connection with immigration should visit many settlements during the past winter. As, for instance, we had to give relief to some people in the northern part of Manitoba, giving certain peonle seed grain
Did you have to give seed grain in Manitoba ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, in some of the unorganized parts of the province in the north, we distributed a little seed grain. The Manitoba government, of course, had full charge in all organized municipalities, acting through the municipal organization. But in the territory which is not municipally organized, in the northern country, there is no provision made, and we had to give a small amount of seed grain taking liens on the homesteads. Throughout the other provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta, where there was a general distribution, of course it was necessary that the services of our officers should be very generally used that the occasion might be met as fully as possible. Hon. gentlemen opposite may perhaps admit that it may turn out that they have been charging to political activity that which was a necessary act in the ordinary transaction of the business of the department.

The minister did n;ot quite understand the drift of my question. Under what authority does this government distribute seed grain in the unorganized parts of Manitoba ? The Bill applied to Alberta and Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Under the same authority as that under whihc we gave relief of the new settlers in the vicinity of Toulon.
Was there any appropriation ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. There is a vote for contingencies which has always been at the disposal of the Immigration Department to meet such cases, and where the amount is not large it is met under that vote. Last year, of course, we had to have a vote of $30,000 to meet the special conditions which existed southwest of Saskatoon. In ordinary years, we are able to meet any cases which may arise out of the vote for contingencies, but this year we were not able to do so. .It is out of that vote that we are allowed to give the relief that we did give at Toulon, in the northern part of Manitoba, and in Saskatchewan.

When the minister is bringing down the information he has promised in respect of the special relief, I would ask him to include all the places he has mentioned, and also to bring down information in regard to repayments of relief given in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There will be no difficulty in bringing down the information in regard to relief given during the past winter, but it would take a considerable amount of research to make a return of repayments that have been made from time to time, because no separate account has been kept of them.
All I wanted was a general idea as to how the money was collected, and to what extent it was being repaid.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There will he no difficulty about giving a general idea.

In regard to officials of the government taking an active part in elections, I would suggest to the minister that he could at least furnish them a strong excuse for abstaining from taking part in elections by putting a clause in the Election Act inflicting a penalty upon any man who takes an active part either on one side or the other.

Genik, the interpreter that I mentioned, was engaged in the municipality of Rosthern where no seed grain was distributed, and consequently there was no excuse for his being there at that particular time. Even had he been engaged in that particular occupation, it was long past the time. The reason why I think it was this man that I refer to, is that one year ago when the provincial elections were going on he was engaged in the same work. I was in the constituency and he was pointed out to me. I know he has been actively engaged in the past, and I think it is the same one.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman give me the name, whoever he was ?
I see in the Auditor General's Report the name of L. B. Cochrane, Medicine Hat, who gets $75 a month as immigration agent. Is he engaged in any other occupation ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is also sub-land agent at Medicine Hat.
Is he not a merchant ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: His son is a merchant.
I think he is head of the firm.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would not necessarily interfere with his employment as a subagent. Almost invariably the persons whom we employ as sub-land agents have some other calling or profession.
A man who gets $75 a month should spend most of his time in the service of the government, without engaging in mercantile pursuits.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far as my knowledge goes of Mr. Cochrane, whatever his other interests may be, he does spend his whole time in the capacity as immigration agent and sub-land agent.
Is there more than one medical health officer in Winnipeg ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Only one.
What is the duty of the inspectors ? I see one, Thomas Cory, of Gladstone, inspector, receiving a pretty large salary. What would be his duties?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is an inspector of British immigrant children, and his salary is provided by the imperial government, under an old arrangement in regard to the immigrant children. We pay him and two or three other inspectors, and we are recouped by the British government. This gentleman resides at Gladstone, and wherever any of these children are located he has to inspect them and report on their treatment.
I see another item about a party of Scotch ploughmen. Give us a little explanation about that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What does the Auditor
General's Report say ?
Expenses in connection with a party of Scotch ploughmen, $110. [DOT]It does not say to whom the money was paid. It may have been paid to Robert Adamson, in Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Adamson some years ago busied himself in going over to Scotland and engaging ploughmen, and bringing them out to the prairie provinces. But

he has not been in that employment for the past three years. I presume the amount of the hon. gentleman finds there is payment of some balance due on former work.
What did these Scotch ploughmen do ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are immigrants, and they engage with farmers in the west. I understood that the men brought out by Mr. Adamson were of a particularly desirable class.
I don't say they were not. The way the item appears here, I do not know whether it means that they were brought out to teach the farmers how to plough.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Adamson went over to Scotland and went into the agricultural districts to get in touch with men who were practical farmers, and men who were ploughmen employed on farms. He brought out ten or twenty of them, and accompanied them to the west and placed them with farmers. They were ordinary Scotch immigrants.

I would like to tell the minister that when I was on the train going from Montreal to Sherbrooke, at Christmas, I met a man whose name I forget, but I think he came from Moose-jaw. He told us that he had been living in the west for twenty years, and was on his way to Scotland to see his friends. He said to us : 'I am not very rich, and a friend of mine came to me and said: ' What will it cost to go to Scotland ?' He told him what it would cost. Well, he says, I will help you.' He said that he went to a man at Moosejaw and this man got him appointed an agent to go to Scotland. He said : The government pays my fare from Moosejaw to Scotland and back again, it pays all my expenses, it gives me $2 a day for my time, from the time I leave home until I get back, and if I get some immigrants to come out with me, I will receive .$2 per head. I heard him say this on the train. He was a Scotchman probably 50 or 55 years of age and he said he had been supporting the government all .his life and it was time he should get some benefit.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I guess he was a Scotchman.

In the Auditor General's Report, page L-29, I see the name of Martin Jerome, Winnipeg, and that he is down for $100 a month or in all $680.64. Martin Jerome comes within the category, I understand, of an active politician. He was a delegate to the Liberal convention in Provencher two months ago, and he was ballotted for in opposition to Mr. OLIVER.
the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Cyr). He seems to be at all the Liberal conventions. He is a very active politician and still he is drawing $100 a month. Then, I see the name, on the same page, of Mr. Thomas McNutt, of Saltcoats, seven and a half months at $125 a month, $937. I have nothing against Mr. MacNutt personally. He is speaker of the Saskatchewan legislature and a most active politician. He could not occupy the position he does as a member of the legislature without being one, and still his name has been figuring in the Auditor General's Report for many years past. I think both these gentlemen come within the category of active politicians, and still they are employees of this government in contravention of the rule laid down by parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Jerome is not now in the employ of the department.
Since when?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Some time last fall he ceased his connection with the department.
What about Thomas MacNutt?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. MacNutt is well known as an old-timer in that locality and he has been employed, not on salary, but from time to time at a per day payment.
He is down here for $125 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At any rate his engagement is not, as I recollect, an engagement at a yearly salary. I am not at all sure what objection there may be to the employment of Mr. MacNutt, but I have always understood that he was a man who stood very well in the community and, although a member of the local legislature, he -was not considered an active or offensive politician.
I think he is an active partisan or he would not be where he is.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Who is the superintendent of the Halifax detention hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Malcolm Chisholm.
At page L-25 of the Auditor General's Report there is an item for the North Atlantic Trading Company of $24,333. Is that the final payment? Does that cover all the arrears?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, that is not the final payment. The final payment is $36,901.50, paid during the year 1907-8.
Was the renewal of the bonus on European immigrants a consequence of the cancellation of the contract with the North Atlantic Trading Company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
To some extent it may be said to have had a connection with that. The agreement with the North (Atlantic Trading Company was brought to an end on November 30, 1906. From that time on there was no bonus paid on immigrants coming from Europe. It will be remembered that the North Atlantic Trading Company agreement did not provide for bonus on immigrants coming from Belgium or France, but only from certain other countries of Europe-Holland, Norway, Sweden, Germany, Austro-Hungary and Russia. After the 30th November, 1906, there was no special inducement for immigrants from any part of Europe. It was thought advisable in the early part of 1907 to adopt in a measure the regulation that prevailed in the British Islands with regard to dealing with European immigration, with the restriction that instead of dealing with ail booking agents we only would deal with the booking agents selected by us in such countries as we 'might feel safe in selecting. That brought France. Holland, Belgium, Norway, Sweden, Germany, Denmark, Finland, Austro-Hungary and Switzerland all under the same provisions as those which existed in England with two exceptions. One was that the bonus was only half what it was for a British immigrant and the other was that we only paid it to selected booking agents instead of to booking agents generally. That system ran on for nearly a year and it was found that it seemed to produce very little result. We found that we were not securing very many of the class of immigrants that we wanted to get and we thought it would be fair to increase the bonus to the same amount as that paid on British immigrants. That is the position as it stands now. Had the North Atlantic Trading Company's contract not been cancelled the present system of bonus would not have been instituted, but this has followed the cancellation of the agreement with the North Atlantic Trading Company. There are some very radical differences between the two arrangements. With the North Atlantic Trading 'Comany there was only nominal restriction as to the classes of immigration. Now the restriction is very definite and strict. Therefore the number upon whom the payment is made is very small. The North Atlantic Trading Company agreement covers all the countries mentioned except France and Belgium. In Russia, Germany, Austro-Hungary and Switzerland we have not yet been able to arrange for booking agents. We have booking agents in France, Belgium, Holland, Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Finland. In these countries we have an arrangement with select booking agents as to the payment of a bonus on the same conditions that we pay the British bonus. A booking agent can only collect bonuses in respect of citizens of the country of which
he himself is a citizen and in which he is operating.

Since the cancellation of the North Atlantic Trading Company contract no bonuses have been paid to immigrants from countries where there are no select booking agents. Has there been any considerable failing off in the immigration from these countries in consequence?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am rather inclined to think there has, but I cannot say definitely at the moment.

I suppose the government will keep careful watch to see whether the bonus system is productive of any increase in immigration. The order in council provides for the payment of the bonus upon navvies or miners who have signified their intention of following farming or railway construction in Canada. Is it sufficient that a navvy should make the mere statement that he intends to pursue farming when he gets to Canada ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The navvy or miner gets no benefit himself from the bonus, and he has no object in making a mis-statement as to his intention. We accept the statement of the booking agent in the old country, and if the statement of the booking agent tallies with the^statement of the immigrant to the agent at our port, the booking agent is entitled to the bonus. But, we are able by our system here to a very great extent to trace our immigrants and if we find that the immigrant does not follow farming we make a deduction of the amount of the bonus from the next payment due to that booking agent. If we find the booking agent has entered into collusion with the man in order to improperly secure the bonus we cease doing business with that agent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the object of advertising in the Christmas numbers of a great many papers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We think it a very satisfactory way of bringing the advantages of Canada before the notice of desirable immigrants. These papers publish a special issue in which the advantages of a particular part of the country are written up, and we purchase a portion of that special issue for distribution through our agencies to the desirable classes. In other cases a newspaper will get out a special issue the circulation of which will be very large and we sometimes advertise in that paper.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What I could not understand precisely was what advantage it was to advertise in a Canadian paper, which presumably is almost entirely circulated in Canada, and could have little or no influence in promoting immigration from foreign countries.

98)60

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is true, but the special number of the ' Globe ' in which we had this advertisement was not a part of the regular issue of the ' Globe ' or sent to its regular subscribers. It was a special issue offered for general sale, and we thought that it was a very creditable representation of Canada, and would be used to a great extent by people who, though living in Canada, have interests in the United States or in England, and who would send copies to their friends in those countries, thereby bringing before them the advantages of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was not alluding more to the Toronto ' Globe ' than to a great many other papers. It seemed to me to be a very indirect way of reaching people abroad. I can understand the purchasing of a large number of copies of a particular issue of some journal and sending them abroad. That is simply another form of immigration literature ; but it does not seem worth while for the department to advertise in these Canadian papers unless it takes some means of assuring the sending of copies of the advertisement abroad. Coming back to special issues of newspapers, have they been pretty thoroughly distributed ? Some time ago the statement was made that a large number of copies of the Halifax ' Chronicle ' which had been purchased, not by this government, but by the Nova Scotia government, had been lying in London for some time and that storage was charged on them. Has anything of that kind occurred under this department ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not say. I think it would be inexcusable if it did. We have plenty of means of distributing these papers. If there was such a ease, I do not pretend to offer the House any excuse for it.

I understand that some time ago the minister ordered the distribution of a million copies of the Winnipeg ' Free Press,' and that reports came from the United States to the effect that a large number of copies were lying in the post offices because there were apparently no such individuals as those to whom they were addressed. Is the minister continuing to order these very large editions of the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' or other papers ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The edition my hon. friend speaks about was gotten out some years ago.
I think two years in succession.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Since I have occupied the position I do not think we have had such an issue as my hon. friend speaks of. In the annual report there is a list of the special editions we have purchased during the Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
preceding year. The largest is one of 36,000 copies of the 1 Northwestern ' a German paper published in Winnipeg.
Where did they go ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They were distributed chiefly among our agencies in the United States. One of the most successful features of our immigration Horn the United States is the German immigration, and I think we have had good value for the money expended.

An enormous amount of money is expended for printing and advertising, a great deal of which seems to be spent in the way of subsidies to party papers. Winnipeg seems to have fared very well in this respect. The Winnipeg ' Canada ' got $591.99, the Winnipeg ' Canadian Hungarian,' $426, the Winnipeg * Loberg,' $1,280, the Winnipeg ' Nordwestern,' $807, the Winnipeg ' Stavel ' Company, $2,214 ; and some of these payments were not at all for special editions, but simply for copies of regular editions. The Toronto ' Globe ' got $10,281, the Halifax ' Chronicle,' $1,132, the Ottawa ' Free Press,' $3,285, the Saskatoon * Phoenix,' $300. Not only have large amounts been paid to newspapers, but any person who has had a fad for getting out any particular article can sell it to the government for immigration purposes. For instance, the Rev. Dr. Bryce, of Winnipeg, got out a book entitled ' Everyman's Geology,' and the government purchased 5,000 copies and paid him $887.50. I do not know what particular influence that book would have in inducing immigrants to come to this country. I have not seen the work, but I know that the Rev. Dr. Bryce has got out several books, and has a faculty of unloading them on the government and the public at very remunerative rates. Rand, McNally and Company, of Chicago, got from the government last year no less than $23,355. No doubt the atlas they got out could not be got out in Canada; but surely some of the printing done in Chicago could be done in Canada. These are only a few items. There is an enormous amount of money paid out for printing and advertising, and I do not know that we have a sufficient return for the outlay. The regular issues of a great many of these weekly papers are of no particular use in the way of inducing immigrants to come to Canada, and a great many of the payments to them are only subsidies.
In nearly every little local paper favourable to this government throughout the western country you will find advertised the homestead regulations. What does that insertion cost?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: I have learned for the first time that there is a distribution of seed grain throughout Manitoba. Where has that been distributed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The distribution is only in that part of the northern section which is not organized into municipalities. The amount distributed was to the value of about $5,000.
In what township and range and who were those who received the grain?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not got the information but there will be no difficulty in giving it. I have already said that we would lay it on the table.
What was the nature of the grain distributed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Principally oats.
Where purchased?
Mr. Castle informed me a short time ago that he purchased a large quantity of oats in Prince Edward Island and also in Scotland and was selling them at 85 cents a bushel.
Who got the seed grain?
I do not know, but no one got any in my district.

Some years ago I was told that when foreign immigrants landed in the locality of a land office, the agents had instructions to hire teams and give assistance in that way to foreigners who wanted to examine the land, but that they were not allowed to do the same for immigrants from the British Isles.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The rule is that if a settler looking for land desires to engage one of the land guides, the settler has to pay the guide for the use of the team. We pay the guide ourselves $2 a day. and that is paid irrespective of the nationality of the applicant.
I was told by a subagent that he had instructions to do that for foreign immigrants only.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The subagent had no warrant for any such statement.
I see in the Auditor General's Report that the government have purchased blankets at $6.50 and $7.50 a pair. That appears pretty expensive. What are those used for?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They have to be purchased for the immigration sheds and hospitals.
Were they bought by tender?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Whom were they bought from?
From Craig & Company, Winnipeg, according to the Auditor General's Report.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They were not bought by tender.
Expenses of deporting undesirable immigrants, $2,000.
How many did you deport last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that since the Medical Act went into force, in 1902, we have deported 1,400.
From what part of Canada have they been deported ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: From all parts. Wherever a complaint has been made we have always acted upon it.
Are they sent from the port of entry, or from any part of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Immigration Act provides that any person who, within two years of his arrival in Canada, becomes subject to certain disabilities, if complaint is made, can be deported on a certain course being taken.
Under what regulations are they deported, and from whom must the information come ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Act provides that, where there is a municipality, the information shall be laid by the clerk of the municipality; elsewhere, the department may act through it own officers. Where there is a municipality we prefer to act on a recommendation or wish of the municipal authorities.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the government bear the whole expense of deportation ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
