speechtext: The law provides that municipalities may be required to share the expense, but, in practice, either the transportation company or the Dominion government bears the expense. I do not think we have had one case in which municipalities have borne a part of the expense.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I may be mistaken, but I have some recollection of a speech made by the provincial secretary of Ontario in which it was shown that considerable expense was incurred by that pro-

vince for deportation. But probably I am mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think It was probably on account of the presence of undesirables.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There was that but I thought there was the other also.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think not.
Can the minister give any idea of the proportion deported by nationalities, showing from what countries we get the desirable and from what country the undesirable immigration ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have not it worked out in that way, and I do not think the result would really give the information my hon. friend desires. It is somewhat dangerous to rest simply on the doctrine of percentage when it comes to a question of the desirability of a number of immigrants.

What disposition was made of the Doukhobors who were taken back to Saskatchewan ? I understood that the provincial government protested to the Dominion government against their return there. Are they being looked after by the provincial authorities, or has the government here any responsibility in the matter ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think I explained on a previous occasion that the position taken by the government is that these people are not immigrants and are outside the immediate control and responsibility of this government. My information is that these people are being dealt with by the provincial government, although i have no definite information on the subject.
Has the provincial government sent in any protest or request in the matter ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have had some communication with the provincial government on the subject; but the position that we took was as I have stated. The law is perfectly clear that, up to a residence of two years in the country, immigrants are under the authority of this government, but, after that, we have no authority over them. It is not a matter of dispute or argument but a matter of fact.

As I understand it, they are being looked after by the Mounted Police. Is not this government in control of the Mounted Police.
Mr. OLIVER, There is a dual authority there. The organization of the force is under the authority of this government, but the force is employed at the jnstance and under the legal authority of the provincial government. So, any duties the Mounted Police may be discharging in Saskatchewan Mr. R. L. BORBEN.
in regard to these people are at the instance and under the authority and direction of the provincial government.
For what reasons may people be deported ? Because they become a public charge ? Is that the only reason ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is one reason. Another is insanity, conviction of crime, or disease.
Mr. SCHAFFNER, Was application made by the city of Toronto recently for a number of young men to be deported ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Last month, something over a hundred men, Bulgarians and Macedonians, were deported from Toronto on complaint of the city that they had become a public charge.

Up to a certain period, immigrants would have to be looked after by the municipal authorities, and it costs them considerable to communicate to this government and have the undesirables deported; Does the government reimburse the municipalities what they have paid ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

From the information we received before the Immigration Committee from the superintendent general, it would appear that there was not sufficient precaution taken at the port of entry to examine these immigrants for disease or anything else which would disqualify them for entry. I believe the information was to the effect that a medical officer would examine 400 immigrants in an hour. Now .it must be an impossibility to make any proper examination of an immigrant in so short a time in order to discover whether he should be admitted under our laws. Perhaps that is one of the reasons why we have had to deport so many. We receive a good deal of information in that committee that would be of advantage to the government in dealing with immigrants, for instance, with regard to the relations between the booking agent and the immigrant. It would seem to me quite natural that when the booking agent and the immigrant meet together the agent should suggest to the immigrant how to answer certain questions, establishing a collusion between them. There also appeared to be a lack of medical supervision at the ports of entry.
It would be interesting if the minister would explain the system of inspection of immigrants who come to Halifax, for instance, in the large ships.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A choice has to be made between care and speed in the inspection

of immigrants at the port of entry. At the present time, in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway boats, the medical officer boards them at Rimouski, and he has the opportunity of looking over the passengers during the trip to Quebec, that is about twelve hours. In the case of the other boats that arrangement has not yet been made, but it appears to be a desirable arrangement and will be extended to all the boats, as all the boats that come to Quebec land at Rimouski. When a vessel lands at Quebec, if the examination has not already been made on the boat the medical officers make an examination of the first and second class passengers immediately. Then flie third-class passengers are landed at the detention sheds and are passed under review as rapidly as possible. If the officer has reason to suspect any physical Imperfection in an immigrant, instead of stopping the line of immigrants until this person has been fully examined, he is sent to the waiting room, and when the main body of passengers have been examined, then the suspected cases are taken up and examined more fully. This gives every reasonable opportunity to the medical man to make a thorough examination. Unless he is absolutely satisfied that the immigrant is all right, he can hold him back and give him a special examination without detaining the great body of passengers. If, after having made the second examination, he finds that his suspicions are confirmed, he may either send the passenger to the hospital or send him back to the country whence he came. When we consider the large number of immigrants who have come out during the past four or five years, we have very little reason to complain of inefficiency in regard to our medical inspection. Just to show that the inspection at the port is to a considerable extent effective, since the Medical Act has gone into force there have been detained in the way I have mentioned at ocean ports 16,000 people and of these over 3,000 have been actually excluded ?
In how many years ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Six years. When you consider the large number of immigrants who have arrived during that time, and when you take the number of deportations and the number of instances where deportation has followed detention, I think it is fair to say that the medical inspection at the ports has been fairly efficient and is becoming more efficient and that there is a reduction in the number of undesirables since the Immigration Act of two years ago was passed which provided for deportation. Before that we did not have the authority to deport. Once the immigrant was landed and entered into Canada we had no authority to send him out, but since the Act providing for deportation came into force there is really very little purpose in an immigrant who is physically unfit attempting to pass the inspection, because even if he does pass the inspecting officer he can be picked up at any place throughout the country within two years and sent home. This deportation provision of the Act is a very drastic provision. It is really heart breaking to enforce it in many cases but it is the only effective way of preventing undesirable immigration. I have every confidence that the deportations which have taken place within the past year or two will have a very manifest effect in checking physically undesirable immigration.
How many have we deported in the past two years after passing the port of entry?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: 1,400 have been deported.
After passing the port of entry?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, that includes people who had come in for two years before. That included four years immigration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Was the Act applied to people who had come into the country before it was passed ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Medical Act which purported to exclude these people went into force in 1902, but the Deportati-on Act of 1900 gave us authority to deport those who should have been excluded.
What about the bonus paid to immigrants who were deported ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In all such cases we charge that amount against the booking agent and deduct it from any future payments that may be made t;o him. If we find he has not been acting in good faith we discontinue business with him.

Does the minister not think that if these immigrants had to produce a certificate of health prior to embarking from the country from which they came it would save a great many of these heart-rending scenes that he speaks about? If they had to undergo a strict examination prior to getting on the vessels by reliable medical men it would save a great deal of trouble and sorrow and avoid the hardships which these people have to endure in travelling thousands of miles to and from their own homes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is something that looks very good on the face of it, but it is not feasible when you come to deal with it. There is just as much difficulty in dealing with the medical examination of immigrants on taking the steamer as there is in

dealing with them on the immigrant leaving the steamer. These people do not live where the steamer sails from. They come from a distance to take that steamer, they come intending to take it immediately and delay at the point of embarkation is just as difficult, in fact it is more difficult to deal with, than delay, at the point of debarkation. Of course, it would be an advantage if that could be done, but there is just the same difficulty in doing it and by only making a medical examination at the port of debarkation the responsibility is thrown absolutely upon the steamboat company. We believe that in the end we will get better results by putting it up to the steamboat company that they shall only carry people who can pass our medical examination. The steamship company do not like to take people back at their own expense. We believe that we will have a more effective check by checking them at the port of debarkation than at the port of embarkation because if they were examined at the port of embarkation the steamship company would be relieved of responsibility.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do the steamship people make a medical examination themselves ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They purport to make a medical examination themselves but it is simply for the purpose of assuring themselves that there is little or no danger of anything occurring during the passage. That is not good enough for our purpose.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: One would suppose that if there is a certain danger of their being put to the expense of taking a large proportion of the immigrants back they would make a medical examination of the same character as that to which the immigrant is subjected on his arrival here.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is our object, and I believe we are in the way of attaining it.
Could you not induce the shipping companies to a frame of mind which would lead them to require medical certificates at the port of embarkation ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are probably getting them to that frame of mind by compelling them to take the immigrants back.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the United States make a medical examination at the port of embarkation ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, at southern European ports, but not at British ports.
If immigrants have been in this country for a year and six months are the steamship companies responsible for their return ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We think it unfair to hold the steamship people responsible for more than a year after the arrival of the immigrant, but if an immigrant were here for over a year we have an arrangement with the steamship companies to take them back at a charity rate which we pay.
What is that rate?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Fifteen dollars across the Atlantic.
Do the booking agents go through the rural districts soliciting immigrants?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Generally they advertise their business, and I understand that a few of them do make such a canvass.

If these agents go to the homes of intending immigrants the medical examination should be made at the originating point. A responsible medical officer in the district should give a certificate which would be presented to the booking agent and*by him to the steamship company. This would save a great deal of trouble to the government and a great deal of distress to immigrants who may be sent back. For what disease is the majority of these immigrants deported? I understand that trachoma is very prevalent and that the disease is spreading and is incurable.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have heard it said that the disease is incurable and I have also heard it is not difficult to cure. In the hospitals which have been established at the ocean ports we give treatment for it, and in a very large number of cases there is said to be complete recovery.

Who can tell whether an immigrant is or is not a farmer so that the booking agent is entitled to the bonus? To my own knowledge men who professed to be farmers knew nothing at all about the business, but no doubt the bonus was paid on them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have already gone oyer that question twice to-night, but for the information of my hon. friend I will go over it again. The booking agent makes his claim, stating that the immigrant has represented himself thus and so to him. That claim is checked against the statement made by the immigrant to the inspecting officer at the point of landing. The ship's manifest shows the name of the immigrant, so that the chain of identification is complete. If it is found that the statement of the immigrant accords with the claim of the booking agent, there is a prima facie case for the payment of the bonus. However, the department has an opportunity of knowledge in regard to the subsequent movements of the immigrant, which is fairly
